messages:
sam_customer: Hey team — after our firewall changes yesterday our Redwood Private inference calls started failing. App gets TLS handshake errors and occasional ECONNRESET. No code changes on our side. We’re on a VPC with NAT gateway and NACLs tightened. Any pointers?

maria_support: sorry you’re hitting this, can you paste the exact error you’re seeing from your app and the timestamp of a failing request? also which flow: inference API traffic to control plane, or inference runtime nodes calling back to control plane?

sam_customer: errors from app (redacted token): 
```
requests.exceptions.SSLError: [SSL: TLSV1_ALERT_UNKNOWN_CA] tlsv1 alert unknown ca (_ssl.c:1123)
requests.exceptions.ConnectionError: ('Connection aborted.', RemoteDisconnected('Remote end closed connection without response'))
```
This is when we call the Redwood private endpoint at https://inference.private.example.com:443 (customer managed ALB in front of Redwood runtime). Failing across multiple instances. Happened right after we tightened NACLs and removed a bunch of ephemeral rules.

alex_infra: quick Qs: is the ALB internet-facing or internal? are you doing TLS termination at ALB or at the backend? also NACLs are stateless — you need explicit ephemeral port ranges allowed for return traffic.

sam_customer: ALB is internal (NLB actually), TLS terminates at the backend containers (they have certs). NACLs applied on the subnet level. We removed broad 1024-65535 allow and only left a short egress bench.

jamie_sre: that lines up — common pitfall: NACLs are stateless so the ephemeral ports used for the client-side source ports (1024-65535) must be allowed inbound/outbound. If you only allow outbound to 443 but block high ports inbound, the TLS handshake will fail. Can you run a quick tcpdump on the backend to see SYN/ACKs?

sam_customer: running tcpdump on one of the app VMs now. Seeing SYN out to 198.51.100.12:443 then no SYN/ACK back, or SYN/ACK but reply reset. snippets: 
```
15:22:11.123456 IP 10.0.2.45.52344 > 198.51.100.12.443: Flags [S], seq 12345, win 64240, options [mss 1460]
15:22:11.223789 IP 198.51.100.12.443 > 10.0.2.45.52344: Flags [S.], seq 54321, ack 12346, win 28960
15:22:11.224000 IP 10.0.2.45.52344 > 198.51.100.12.443: Flags [R], seq 12346, win 0
```
So the remote is replying but our host resets the connection. Could that be NACL?

maria_support: interesting — that pattern (S then S. then immediate R from client) is often the client kernel refusing the packet because it doesn't see the NAT translation match or it's out-of-state for conntrack. On AWS, the NACL might allow the inbound S. but if outbound ephemeral ports are blocked earlier you might see resets. Two things to check: (1) NACL rule order and both directions for ephemeral range, (2) backend host conntrack table (run `sudo conntrack -L | grep 198.51.100.12`), (3) ensure your NAT gateway is healthy and not cycling source ports.

alex_infra: also confirm NACL entries numeric order — lowest rule number matched first. Example NACL entries you likely need (for outbound from private subnet):
```
Rule 100: ALLOW TCP 0.0.0.0/0 -> 443 (egress)
Rule 110: ALLOW TCP 0.0.0.0/0 -> 1024-65535 (ephemeral egress)
Rule *: DENY ALL
```
And mirrored inbound rules that allow 443/ephemeral to your subnet source CIDRs. Note: AWS NACLs require explicit allow for return high ports. Security groups are stateful so they handle return by themselves.

sam_customer: we only had 443 allowed outbound and inbound allowed 443 too. I’ll add 1024-65535 to both inbound and outbound and test. Any quick command to verify reachability to the control plane handshake before we flip NACLs?

jamie_sre: try from a host in the same subnet: `curl -vI https://inference.private.example.com:443 --resolve inference.private.example.com:198.51.100.12` or `openssl s_client -connect 198.51.100.12:443 -servername inference.private.example.com -msg` — that will show the handshake steps. Also `traceroute -T -p 443` to see path.

sam_customer: ran `openssl s_client` and it hangs at `SSL_connect:errno=0` then eventually error. After adding ephemeral 1024-65535 allow to NACL inbound+outbound, tests improved. `curl -v` now gets HTTP 200.

maria_support: awesome — so likely NACL was dropping the return path or client conntrack reset. For posterity, two gotchas we see: (1) on-prem firewalls may also enforce ephemeral ranges differently (check appliance sessions), (2) AWS Network Load Balancer preserves source IPs so your backend sees client ports — ensure your backend OS firewall allows ephemeral replies.

sam_customer: note: we also had a host-level iptables rule that was too strict (`DROP all -- 198.51.100.12 anywhere`), so between the NACL change and relaxing the iptables we got stable. Thanks.

alex_infra: can you paste the final NACL rules you applied so we can add to KB?

sam_customer: sure — final minimal rules we used (applied both inbound and outbound):
```
100 ALLOW TCP 0.0.0.0/0 443
110 ALLOW TCP 0.0.0.0/0 1024-65535
120 ALLOW UDP 0.0.0.0/0 1024-65535
* DENY ALL
```

maria_support: saved — adding to support KB: note about stateful SG vs stateless NACL ephemeral ranges + iptables traps. Also adding an example `tcpdump` filter to detect resets: `sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 host 198.51.100.12 and tcp`

deploy-bot: [deploy] KB updated: `support/kb/nacl-ephemeral-return-traffic.md` :white_check_mark:

sam_customer: everything green now, thanks team :tada:
